payload.props_realized:
Both realized, and each killer story maps to the prop whose failure would void it.

PROP 1 (the agent walking the loop) is realized by S1 (KILLER - consult what the process demands, covering N1/N2/N5), S3 (a law minted today binds a session tomorrow, N3) and S4 (a mechanical change is one call, N4). All five of Prop 1's needs are carried.

PROP 2 (the owner who owns an iteration they did not watch) is realized by S2 (KILLER - a gate judges itself where it can, N6/N9), S5 (the record survives carelessness, N8) and S6 (a check that cannot decide does not stop the night, N7). All four needs carried.

No prop is realized only by a non-killer story, and no story exists without a prop - the check that would catch invented scope.
payload.stories_generalized:
Every story sits inside a use case, and the mapping is not one-to-one on purpose - the use cases generalize across stories where the underlying goal is the same.

UC-A covers S1 and S3: consulting a source and receiving the rules that bind the step are the same user goal - the agent is acquiring what it needs to work correctly, whether that is a document or a law.
UC-B covers S4.
UC-C covers S2 and S6: the happy path and the deferral path of the same goal, which is why S6 lives as UC-C's extension 2a rather than as its own case - a lint that defers is not a different goal, it is the same gate behaving correctly under a limit.
UC-D covers S5.

The extensions carry the weight: 3b (source only in history), 4b (a malformed request must REFUSE rather than coerce), 2a in UC-B (one bad guard applies nothing), 2a and 3b in UC-C (defer, and a wrongly-failing lint is reportable), 3a in UC-D (the remote force-push is an owner act). Those are where this iteration's actual value sits - the refusal paths, not the happy ones.
payload.roles_covered:
Nine roles, none left out, and the map deliberately SPLITS the owner into three - adjudicator, auditor and operator - because they need different things and one design decision (delegation) serves the first while threatening the second.

Six tensions named with rulings: T1 walking vs arriving agent on guidance volume (ruled: serve the arriving agent, since it cannot recover what it never received); T2 walking agent vs auditor on speed against traceability (ruled: the lane must WIN rather than prohibit, because a prohibition that can be routed around produces exactly the silent reads the auditor loses); T3 adjudicator vs auditor - the same person, opposed interests, resolved by se.law-responsibility-never-delegates: computing the mechanical half is what lets the adjudicator leave AND serves the auditor; T4 operator vs the no-fallback ruling, NAMED NOT RESOLVED because the owner made that trade knowingly; T5 the engine itself vs everyone, since self-hosting means rewriting the tools being used to rewrite; T6 the retro vs everyone, deliberately under-served here because log hygiene is a named non-goal.

ONE HONEST GAP, recorded rather than glossed: no tension was found involving the future iteration, and a design nobody objects to usually means a role is missing. The role I am least confident I have represented is the operator on a platform I have never tested - which is precisely where the no-fallback ruling bites.
payload.excluded_stated: Yes, at draw_context, system-level and binding - twelve lines, each naming something the system does NOT do, sharper than M1's vision-level non-goals. The load-bearing ones for this iteration: no index over product files (freshness, not cost); no second search implementation (owner ruling); no writes outside the product except se_config into the machine-local dir; no lint that judges intent; no lint with a third outcome; no push, force-push or history rewrite; and no fix for the trunk/worktree gap however often it bites. The list is what a later state gets measured against when scope tries to grow.
payload.examples_formulated:
The formulated examples are named and their status is stated honestly.

EVERY SLIDE of every story is a formulated example, and the use-case scenario paths generalize them. The ones that will become CHECKABLE, and are therefore the ones worth naming now: S1 slides 2-4 (read a 132k file in parts; search v1 by ref with context; find a term that exists only in a closed iteration's evidence) - each is directly executable. S4 slides 2-3 (six edits, one atomic call, one recorded change). S5 slides 1-2 (delete every tag, evidence still reachable by hash) - executable and destructive, so it runs against a fixture rather than the real record. S6 slides 2-3 (a check that cannot decide defers, the run continues) - executable by planting an undecidable check.

S2's slides are the ones I cannot fully formulate yet, and I am saying so rather than pretending: 'the lint has already compared what the build touched against what the architecture allocated' presumes a machine-readable allocation, and whether the M4 element allocation IS machine-readable is not yet known. That question goes to M5 as a spike rather than being assumed here - if it is not readable, S2's slide 2 becomes a different check and the story changes.

Examples stay roles-and-prose here; they become nodes at M3 where the requirements source to them.
